resources.string: The picture in the scan step
This file has no scan data this screen can edit. It may be progressive, or already damaged.
No bit in this stretch of the row changed the picture or stayed readable. Flip moves on from them next press.

The scan data is the picture itself - the coded bits of every block - rather than a table describing it. The quantization and Huffman screens say how to read those bits; this screen changes them. A flip here is a JPEG glitch at its rawest: a bit that was 0 becomes 1, and the decoder reads on from there without ever being told anything went wrong.
What a press of flip does

A flip walks the row rather than sampling it: the first press tries the row\'s first byte, the next press the second, and when the row runs out the bit position moves along a place and it starts again. Bits that leave the picture identical or stop the file decoding are skipped, so a press lands on the next bit that actually changes something. The same row and the same presses still write the same file, and each press can be undone on its own.
The row it is aimed at

The first slider picks the row a press lands in: one row of 8x8 blocks, not one row of pixels. The slider steps from section to section rather than sliding through fractions, and the readout under it counts those sections.
The chosen section is where the next press lands. It is not a limit on where the damage spreads.
How far one bad bit travels

A decoder has no way to know a bit is wrong, so inside a run of data it keeps decoding and one wrong bit can carry the error to the end of the scan. Restart markers are what stop it: the encoder is allowed to start again at each one, so damage cannot cross one. Most photos straight from a camera carry none at all.
One wrong bit, and the damage running until the next marker stops it.

The second slider sets how tall a band the damage should be confined to, as a fraction of the picture, and the button rebuilds the scan with markers at that spacing. Once a file has them, the line above says how many it carries and the slider is replaced by that.

Flip writes the next bit along that changes the picture, Undo takes the last press back a press at a time - an injection comes back in one press too, however many bytes it moved - and Reset goes all the way back to the file this screen was handed. All three grey out when there is nothing for them to do, and stay where they are rather than coming and going.

Next hands on what this screen has made of the file, and goes on to the final preview, where it is saved, shared or written as another format. Leaving the bytes alone is reset followed by next: the flips are the whole of what this screen does to them.

The triangle after the title opens the Huffman tables, which are the other half of what a code means: the tables say which symbol each code stands for, and this screen changes the codes themselves. They are a screen of their own because one rewritten symbol can change whole runs of blocks at once, and they open on the file as this screen has made it, flips and all.

Restart markers are never flipped: a byte changed inside one is a different marker, which is a different file rather than a glitched one. Bytes whose every flip would make the file undecodable are skipped, and the panel says how many; on top of that a press skips individual bits whose result is pixel-identical or does not open. A progressive JPEG, or a scan that is already damaged, has nothing this screen can safely edit, and it says so instead of offering a flip.

I was curious about what happens if you corrupt random bits in a JPEG file. It started with a python prototype to validate the idea. The results were interesting, so I decided to make an Android app out of it. This allowed me to get a deeper understanding of JPEG files and document it within the app. The UI was challenging and I feel it is still not optimal, but it is good enough to release.
Instead of flipping bits at random we edit the parts of a JPEG that decide what the picture looks like:
How roughly each pattern inside a block is kept.
One bad bit travels until a restart marker stops it.
Rewrites what each code stands for. One symbol can change what whole runs of blocks decode to.
Moves the average of every 8x8 block: the picture gets brighter or darker.
Moves the average color of every block: colors pull apart or wash together.
Horizontal bands, in color only (chroma table).
Vertical bands, in color only (chroma table).
Squares in both directions: a checkerboard when u equals v, a plaid when they differ.
Squares in both directions, in color only (chroma table).
Fine patterns need detail in the photo: rows that would change nothing are hidden.
One number for every block. Turn the wheel or tap the arrows to step it one at a time.
Block average - moves the whole picture

JPEG does not store pixels. It splits the photo into 8x8 blocks, describes each block with 64 numbers, and the quantization tables (DQT) say how roughly each of those numbers is kept. Editing them changes how the photo is stored, not what was photographed.
The 64 DCT basis patterns of an 8x8 block

Every square below is one of those 64 numbers, drawn as the pattern it adds to each block: how much it wiggles, and in which direction. The top-left is flat, so it only moves the block\'s average. The further right and down, the finer the detail it carries.
Which square belongs to which button
The flip screen sorts those squares into four families:
Each family exists twice: the luma table (drawn here) and the chroma table, whose buttons carry the word color. The color families tint the picture instead of adding brightness detail.
Each number is divided by its quantizer when the file is written and multiplied back when it is read, so a bigger quantizer keeps less of that pattern:
kept finely - the pattern stays smooth
kept roughly - the pattern flattens into bands

JPEG does not store individual pixels. It cuts the picture into squares of 8 by 8 pixels no matter the width and height of the picture. Every glitch the app makes lands inside those squares, so they are also the shape of what you see when a file is corrupted.

Number of squares is determined by the width and height of your picture as pixels. A lower number divided by 8 will give you a lower square count: bigger squares when rendered edge to edge and a more grid like appearance.

Every edit requires the whole file to be decoded again to show you the result. The work is proportional to the number of squares. Halving the width and the height leaves a quarter of the squares and a quarter of the work.

The slider picks the width of the resized photo you will be working with. The crop buttons pick the frame it is exported in: No crop keeps the picture\'s own shape, 1:1 trims it to a square, and 9:16 is the frame stories take. Drag the picture to move the crop and pinch to zoom it; whatever is outside the bright frame is left out.

The code book behind the picture

JPEG does not store coefficients as numbers. For every 8x8 block it writes a string of Huffman codes, and each code stands for a symbol that says how far along the block to jump and how many bits the value needs. The Huffman tables are the dictionary those codes are read with: the quantization tables say how roughly the picture was kept, these say how it was written down.
A table in the file is a header, then a list of symbols. The header names the table and gives the length of every code; the list says what each code means, in code order.
Sixteen counts: how many codes of each length
The symbols, in code order - the only part this screen edits

Every bit of the name byte and of the sixteen counts makes the file undecodable, so this screen never offers them: the decoder reads as many symbols as the counts ask for, and a flip in a count breaks that agreement with the list that follows.
A code is as loud as it is short

Codes are handed out by frequency: the shortest code goes to the pair of values the picture produces most often. That is what makes the position in the list the strength control - editing symbol #0 changes thousands of blocks, and editing #150 changes nothing at all.
Every code of the luma detail table. The tall bright bars on the left are short codes, used constantly; the flat tail is 125 codes these photos never emit.

In the detail tables a symbol packs two numbers into one byte: how many zero coefficients to skip, and how many bits the next value needs. The first coefficient of a block is coded separately, so each row below starts just after it.
Skip a few, then one four-bit value: the common case, and the one this code was designed for.
Skip nine, then one two-bit value: the same code, told to jump much further along the block.
Two of these symbols do something special. A skip of 0 with a size of 0 ends the block; a skip of 15 with a size of 0 means sixteen zeros in a row.

In the two level tables the symbol is not a pair but a single number: how many bits the block level takes. The decoder reads exactly that many bits after every code, so changing one of these symbols puts the whole rest of the scan out of step - which is why they hit the picture far harder than a detail edit of the same size.
Two kinds of edit are left out entirely, because no picture comes out of them.
Every bit of a code length count. A changed count either overruns the table or leaves bytes over that the decoder then reads as the next table.
A level symbol of 16 or more. A block level cannot need more bits than the sample size, and past 15 the decoder stops on the stream.

Most of a table is usually dead weight. On the four sample photos only 77 of the luma detail table\'s 162 codes are ever emitted, and 45 of the color detail table\'s - so most of the available edits cannot change anything on that photo. This screen counts that per image and hides the dead ones.

A code being used is not the same as a visible change. Skipping one more coefficient, or reading one bit more, can land inside what the encoder already rounded away - two thirds of the sample batch measured as no visible change at all.
Detail edits in the color table register in the color channels rather than the brightness; the level tables move brightness on the luma side and color on the chroma side.
This picture has not been saved.
The glitched file exactly as it is — nothing is decoded or encoded again.
The picture decoded and written again as a JPEG, so it is smaller than raw — but it is no longer the bytes your flips made.
Lossless, but the picture is decoded and written again as a PNG.
The smallest of the three, and lossy: the picture is decoded and written again.
Could not write the picture as %1$s.
Allow storage access to save the picture.

By the time this screen appears the picture is finished. The resize screen set its size and crop, the quantization screen set how roughly each frequency is kept, and the scan screen flipped bits in the scan data - and the Huffman tables were retuned from that screen, if they were retuned at all. All this screen decides is what file those bytes leave the app as, and where the file goes.
Four choices, two kinds of file

Raw JPEG is not re-encoded at all: the bytes handed to save or share are the bytes the flips made, exactly. That is the point of glitching a JPEG - the damage is in those bytes, and copying them costs nothing. The other three are built from the decoded picture instead: a plain JPEG at the app\'s own quality, or a PNG or a WebP, each written out again with the damage redrawn into pixels. They read the same and they are not the same file - and it is a one-way trip, because encoding a glitched picture to a PNG does not give you something you can come back and edit here later.
Saving, sharing, and where things go

Save writes the file into Pictures/Glitch. Share saves nothing: it puts a copy in the app\'s own cache and hands it to whichever app you pick, and that app decides what it keeps. The two are independent, so a picture can be sent without ever reaching the gallery. Restart is the first button: it leaves all of this behind and goes back to the picker for another photo, asking first while the file has not been saved.
